It proceeds through two phases: induction (the chemical penetrates the skin, reacts covalently with skin proteins to form hapten-protein conjugates, which are processed by dendritic cells and presented to T cells, priming the adaptive immune system) and elicitation (subsequent exposure triggers a T cell-mediated inflammatory response). The key molecular event is haptenation — covalent modification of skin proteins by the chemical or its metabolite.

For a chemical to act as a skin sensitizer, it must: (1) penetrate the stratum corneum (the skin's outer barrier), (2) be electrophilic or become electrophilic after abiotic or enzymatic activation in the skin, and (3) react covalently with nucleophilic amino acid residues (primarily cysteine thiol and lysine amine) on skin proteins. The reaction mechanism determines the sensitization potency — strong electrophiles that react with both cysteine and lysine (e.g., acid anhydrides, isocyanates) tend to be stronger sensitizers than those reacting with only one nucleophile.

Structural features associated with skin sensitization: Michael acceptors (α,β-unsaturated carbonyls, acrylates, methacrylates — react with cysteine via 1,4-addition). Acylating agents (acid anhydrides, acid chlorides, isocyanates, isothiocyanates — react with lysine amines). Context: Carcinogenicity is the ability of a substance to cause cancer through sustained genetic damage, epigenetic changes, or chronic disruption of cellular growth control. This dataset (Lagunin) classifies compounds as carcinogens or non-carcinogens based on long-term rodent bioassay data (typically 2-year studies in rats and mice), which is the regulatory gold standard for carcinogenicity assessment.

Carcinogenicity can arise through genotoxic or non-genotoxic mechanisms. Genotoxic carcinogens directly damage DNA — this overlaps substantially with Ames mutagenicity but also includes clastogens (chromosome breakers) and aneugens (spindle poisons) that are not detected by the Ames test.
